fixes.explanation: That rescue belongs to Abimelech's father, not to Abimelech. Jotham later says his father fought for Shechem and risked his life to deliver them from the hand of Midian (Judges 9:17). Back in verse 3, the leaders give a much simpler reason: "He is our brother." Family, not rescue.

It's true, baker. Jotham says the leaders made Abimelech, the son of his father's maidservant, king over the leaders of Shechem. His reason is "…because he is your brother…" The leaders said almost the same thing back in verse 3: "He is our brother."

Actually, it's true. The text says Abimelech took the silver and hired some "…worthless and reckless men to follow him." Seventy shekels of silver from the temple of Baal-berith paid for them. So True is the answer.
Yes. Jotham survived because he hid himself. The text gives that reason and no other. I think he had a lot to carry after it.

Good guess, since the book is called Judges. Don't let the name fool you, friend. Here the leaders of Shechem and Beth-millo gathered beside the oak at the pillar and proceeded to make Abimelech their king. That's the title the text gives him, and it isn't judge.
No priest in this verse, friend. The leaders gather beside the oak at the pillar and make Abimelech their king. King is the only title the verse gives him.

Yes, Jotham climbs to the top of Mount Gerizim, raises his voice and cries out. His first words are, "Listen to me, O leaders of Shechem, and may God listen to you." I think a man who hid while his brothers were murdered has decided he's done staying quiet.
Mount Tabor shows up elsewhere in Judges. In Deborah's story, Barak went up Mount Tabor (Judges 4:12). Jotham's mountain is Gerizim.

The olive tree says, "Should I stop giving my oil that honors both God and man, to hold sway over the trees?" Its answer is a question, and it's a no in disguise. The olive tree won't give up its oil to hold sway over the trees. I think it'd rather keep making oil than rule.
Oil belongs to the olive tree, the first one the trees ask. The grapevine's gift is wine, the kind that cheers both God and man. Good guess, just a different tree.

Shade comes up later, and it's the thornbush who talks about it. The grapevine says it won't stop giving its wine that cheers both God and man. So you've got the right story, just a different speaker.
The text doesn't say altar. Jotham says the seventy sons were killed on a single stone. I think this one hurts, and it's heavy. The text just says it plainly.

Beer. After his message from Mount Gerizim, Jotham ran away, escaping to Beer, and he lived there. That's where this passage leaves him. I think after speaking up like that, he didn't hang around for the replies.

Yes. The text says Jotham "…lived there for fear of his brother Abimelech." Abimelech is the brother who murdered his seventy brothers, so I think that fear makes sense. Fear is the reason the text gives for his staying in Beer.
